A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cultural-bias study and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained experiments can be matched despite substantial changes to evaluation coverage and presentation.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of off-the-shelf VLMs, controlled experiments with six mLLaVA variants, evaluator validation and hidden-state probing.

after.justification: v2 reports original VLM evaluations and controlled experiments, including revised objective-task results, human agreement measurements and a refusal analysis.

M1.justification: Both versions train the same six mLLaVA variants using CLIP, Llama2/Baichuan2 and English, Chinese or bilingual fusion corpora, following the same LLaVA/LoRA recipe. Changes to judges and task prompts concern evaluation procedures rather than the proposed model construction.

E1.justification: Dollar Street expands from US/China coverage to English/Chinese-speaking and broader regional country groups. VQAv2/VLUE are replaced by A-OKVQA/CVQA, introducing additional countries and culturally diverse question-and-answer authorship, whereas v1's VQA annotations were English-authored. ArtELingo and the fusion-training corpora remain.

E2.justification: The off-the-shelf comparison shrinks from ten models to six: BLIP2-OPT-7B, LLaVA-0-Llama-7B, LLaVA-1-Llama-7B and mBLIP-mT0-XL disappear. v2 also excludes BLIP2-Flan-T5-XXL from Chinese-prompted evaluations. The appendix evaluator comparison changes from Mistral versus GPT-4 against human judgments to Prometheus versus human-human agreement.

E3.justification: VQA changes from open-answer correctness judgments to four-option prompting and Mistral candidate extraction, including translation of Chinese generations into English. Object identification replaces Mistral's binary judgment with Prometheus-2-8x7B rubric scores, averaged over five judgments and thresholded at 3. Human validation changes from 160 object-identification and 240 VQA generations to 200 object-identification generations with two raters per language.

E4.justification: v2 adds a refusal analysis, finding fewer than 0.1% of mLLaVA generations meet its refusal criteria, and revises evaluator validation to examine human-human and human-Prometheus agreement by language and image country. The three language-factor ablations and logit-lens investigation remain; the new probing table largely documents the existing analysis.

E5.justification: v2 adds five stochastic judge evaluations per object-identification answer and reports their mean, plus Cohen's kappa and human-human agreement in Table 2. The two-factor significance-testing approach and 0.05 threshold remain unchanged. These additions concern evaluator reliability, not additional model-training runs.

E6.justification: Objective-task and off-the-shelf results are extensively revised. For example, Chinese prompting changes monolingual Baichuan2's Dollar Street bias from 1.103 to 1.094 in v1, but from 1.074 to 1.190 in v2's en/zh evaluation. These use different coverage and judges, so this is a changed finding rather than a same-setting deterioration. Reported off-the-shelf bias reductions change from 27/40 to 15/30 comparisons under different model/task sets. All mLLaVA ArtELingo entries match between v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 6.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(2) retain the equal-performance criterion and Western-to-comparison-group performance ratio. Geographic labels change, but no substantive mathematical definition, derivation or proof changes. The expanded logit-lens description explains an existing technique.

C1.justification: The central claims about language pre-training, prompting and the limitations of multilingual fusion remain. v2 explicitly extends its claims to neighboring-country groups and strengthens contribution 4 to significant reductions on both objective and subjective tasks; v1 emphasized significance for subjective tasks. The fifth contribution about fusion restates a claim already present in v1.

C2.justification: The new Ethics Statement explains stereotyping risks and why English/Chinese cannot fully represent the regional cultures studied, extending v1's brief proxy caveat. Appendix A.3.1 newly discusses tokenizer differences and unavailable corpus-composition and alignment details when defending Llama2/Baichuan2 comparability. The main mechanistic interpretation remains.

D1.justification: The appendix substantially expands scoring rubrics, annotation instructions, answer-extraction fallback rules, translation-validation details and base-model architecture information. v2 also reports model availability on HuggingFace. Conversely, v1's evaluation sample counts and explicit ArtELingo test-set versus full-corpus allocation disappear. The LoRA training, hardware and training-time disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for the replacement benchmarks, Prometheus 2, self-consistency, cultural regionalization and other supporting topics, while dropping the VQAv2/VLUE references. Its discussion additionally addresses multilingual retrieval through Ramos et al. and translation through Qiu et al. The central positioning against prior work focused on image distributions is unchanged.

P1.justification: The title changes, and substantial rewriting affects the abstract, introduction, task descriptions and results narrative. Methods are regrouped around the two study steps, the appendix is reorganized into detailed task/evaluation/training/probing sections, and Ethics and Reproducibility Statements are added. Terminology consistently shifts from Eastern to East Asian.

P2.justification: The paper switches from two-column to single-column formatting. v1's absolute-performance scatterplot is removed, bias plots are rebuilt with regional panels, and Figures 1-3 are revised. The dataset table is redesigned and moved into the main text. Architecture, raw probing and off-the-shelf score tables are added, while the controlled-results table is expanded and renumbered.

improvement.justification: Broader country comparisons and locally authored VQA annotations provide more informative evidence about cultural generalization. Human-human calibration of the evaluator, the refusal check and explicit comparability limitations also improve transparency. These gains are tempered by the loss of evaluation sample counts and ArtELingo split-selection details, while uncertainty about base-model comparability remains. The evidence supports a limited net improvement.
